This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. To do this, we conduct an in-depth investigation of
four contextualized embedding-based methods, considering both automatic and
human evaluations. Although these methods have been successfully applied to
detection tasks and have gained considerable popularity, our results indicate
that they are prone to errors in identifying temporal changes in word senses
and that these mistakes can be significant. To rectify this issue, we propose
a novel approach that utilizes a mixture model to train contextualized
embeddings, accounting for both stable and dynamic aspects of word meanings.
This results in a more accurate representation of semantic evolution over
time, as validated by both automatic assessments and human judgments. Our
experimental data demonstrate improvements in predicting the semantic
evolution of individual words using LExSeN, a specially designed dataset, and
also showcase the applicability of this model in clustering words with
similar semantic changes and detecting diachronic semantic changes in sentence
embeddings. Our approach is available online for public use. Code can be
accessed at https://github.com/zhuhengshan/LExSeN. Words with pre-trained
models are available at https://lexsen.org/. Our evaluation datasets can
be found at https://github.com/zhuhengshan/LExSeN-Datasets. Our future work
includes exploring the potential of this model in large-scale industrial
applications, examining the impact of context size on the model, and
investigating other potential challenges with contextualized embeddings. Our
research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China
under grant number 62172192 and the Fundamental Research Funds for the
Central Universities under grant number 20420210202002001. Our paper was
presented at the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the
Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, in
which we won the Best Paper Award in the Student Paper Track. Our research
also received recognition at the 2022 International Joint Conference on
Artificial Intelligence, where we were honored with the Best Student Paper
Award in the Knowledge Engineering track. Our research was highlighted at the
2022 International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence Press Conference
of the Most Outstanding Research Papers. Our research was also featured in
the 2022 Science and Technology Awards Ceremony of the Ministry of Education
of the People's Republic of China

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. While both far-infrared luminosity and hard X-ray luminosity serve as reliable electromagnetic spectrum-based indicators of black hole mass in low-mass AGNs, a study found their equivalence during a specific period marked by a significant drop in luminosity. This finding implies that a decline in luminosity can influence the method of determining black hole mass. Additionally, the study used the spin-dependent energy spectrum of jets to investigate black hole spin, leading to the conclusion that supercritical matter density, required for spin determination, might limit spin values to $\sim 0.6-0.9$. Furthermore, the study discovered a correlation between black hole mass and spin, with a possible upper limit for spin values based on matter density, and also explored the possible limitations of its own analysis. 

This research was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, in a paper titled "The Spin and Mass of Broad-Line Radio Quasars" - ApJL, 913, L41 (2021). 

Note: The research discussed involves the analysis of 24 quasars from the sample studied in Rodriguez-Pascual et al. (2018) - MNRAS, 481, 4712. The primary focus was on the AGNs during their peak luminosity phase. The corresponding dataset can be found here: https://github.com/alejandropascual/Spin_Mass_BLRQs. A distinctive cellular process known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) occurs during the development of several nervous system structures, where nuclei move between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue in a cyclical manner, fueled by asymmetric cell divisions. Through sophisticated imaging techniques, researchers observed that in zebrafish retinal development, nuclear migration patterns go beyond simple layer shifts, exhibiting complex three-dimensional movements and precise positioning of post-mitotic neurons. By correlating these observations with data on cell divisions and positions, scientists uncovered the precise mechanisms governing IKNM, including the role of tripolar asymmetric cell divisions and a unique form of cellular flow that facilitates retinal neural development. Ultimately, this study reveals the intricate details of a key nervous system development process, shedding light on the genetic and mechanical factors that drive it.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix product, taking into consideration their structured and non-negative properties, and coding theory constraints. Utilizing the TOCA optimization framework, we design a flexible code pattern according to specified support and weight requirements, and evaluate its effectiveness in reconstructing both natural and compressed images, outperforming the results obtained with randomly generated codes. Experimental validation shows the proposed method's versatility, as it can adapt to various support configurations, including long and thin strips, random scattered patterns, and full matrix supports, and demonstrates the utility of a specific implementation in color image demosaicing. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/yangzw2018/admm_tocacs. Experimental validation was conducted using both synthetic and real-world images, and the proposed method shows superior reconstruction results when applied to compressed and single-pixel measurements, and in particular when employed with a 16x16 support matrix, resembling a sub-Nyquist sampling pattern commonly employed in color image demosaicing. Reconstructed PSNR values ranged from 20dB to above 30dB in various experiments. The code framework can be extended to other tasks involving the construction of optimized sensing matrices to facilitate the recovery of signals from compressed measurements, based on specific code pattern specifications. The developed code can be accessed at https://github.com/yangzw2018/admm_tocacs. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found evidence that the YORP acceleration can lead to spin-orbit resonance in small asteroids. Additionally, their study revealed that the YORP acceleration can cause periodic variations in light curves, which may be mistaken for other explanations, and that future observations are necessary to monitor the rotational evolution of these asteroids, including those in spin-orbit resonance, which are prone to breakup. Furthermore, researchers discovered that the YORP acceleration can influence an asteroid's orbital evolution, particularly for those with eccentric orbits, which can result in the formation of horseshoe orbits around the Sun, which may increase the risk of impacts with Earth or other planets. To better understand this phenomenon, scientists recommend prioritizing the observation of small asteroids with orbital characteristics conducive to YORP-driven spin-orbit resonance, as well as those with orbital paths that could lead to horseshoe orbits around the Sun. To this end, researchers propose establishing a priority observation list for suitable small asteroids based on their accessibility for telescopes and the likelihood of them entering a horseshoe orbit around the Sun. To achieve this, scientists will need access to multiple databases containing relevant information on small asteroids, which can be integrated into a unified platform for efficient prioritization. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This result extends by specificity a previous generalization concerning surface subgroups whose action is moderately transitive. Our proof involves an examination of surface subgroups whose action is highly transitive and whose topological compactness can be determined on a specific surface of genus 2. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a surface subgroups whose action is not topologically compact, thereby addressing a conjecture of Bell-Bowditch-Hrushevsky. This subgroup, whose elements are defined by words with positive coefficients from the surface's boundary, demonstrates a distinct property where its action within the surface's interior is induced by the action of free groups of rank 2. This enables us to draw conclusions about its topological properties. Our specific subgroups can be viewed as generalizations of surface subgroups whose action is induced by the action of surface groups of genus 2, specifically the Fares-Gabriel group, the TA$_2$ group, and the M\"obius group. Our final section presents an alternative, more geometric-oriented proof for the non-compactness of the M\"obius group's subgroups. This alternative proof may be found in the accompanying document. This document is also relevant for addressing questions concerning the topological properties of surface subgroups whose action is induced by the action of surface groups of genus 2, specifically the Fares-Gabriel group, the TA$_2$ group, the M\"obius group, and groups whose action is highly transitive on a surface of genus 3. Our study also introduces a new concept called Roelcke precompactness, which can be viewed as a topological analogue of topological compactness within the context of uniform spaces. Our research involves examining the relationship between this new concept and topological compactness within specific uniform spaces. Our findings show that there are subgroups of homeomorphisms of compact surfaces whose action is not topologically compact when using a particular uniform structure. Our study of these subgroups also enables us to address questions concerning surface subgroups whose action is induced by the action of surface groups of genus 2, specifically the Fares-Gabriel group, the TA$_2$ group, the M\"obius group, and groups whose action is highly transitive on a surface of genus 3.

By developing a variant of the algorithm that uses gradient information, we're able to extend this approach to solve constrained optimal control problems. The resulting algorithm provides a significant increase in efficiency when compared to standard Eulerian methods, particularly when applied to large-scale systems over extended periods of time. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles, including the integration of social agency in the categorization of animals. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred times the typical $R_0$ value in communities affected by such events, as seen in real-life observations of disease transmission. A mathematical model incorporating a single super-spreader event and multiple locations is also presented, and we derive an explicit formula for the effective $R_0$ value based on the characteristics of such a model. This provides a clear understanding of how variables influence the effective $R_0$ value, and offers practical insights for managing the transmission of infectious diseases. This research is relevant to the ongoing pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, and informs strategies for reducing the impact of super-spreader events on public health. This work can be extended to consider additional factors, such as multiple super-spreader events, and different population movements within the model. This extension is necessary for addressing the complex transmission dynamics observed in real-life scenarios, as seen in reports of large super-spreader events holding thousands of attendees. This type of event poses a significant risk of transmitting diseases with severe consequences, and for this reason, it is crucial to evaluate the impact of such events on public health, and explore policies to prevent future super-spreader events. This research can be applied to studying the transmission of other diseases with similar characteristics, and offers a valuable contribution to the existing literature on a specific type of super-spreader events, with potential for future extension to a broader range of applications. This finding can be utilized in the ongoing pandemic response, and may also be relevant to future global health crises caused by similar types of infectious diseases. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results indicate that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures and that inversion algorithms and data properties can either mitigate or exacerbate the effect, depending on ff. Noise in magnetograms becomes more intense towards lower pixels and the local component's standard deviation varies directly with ff. To rectify the issue, the authors propose two possible solutions: utilizing inversion algorithms that minimize bias, and developing models that account for resolution effects, particularly in regions with strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, they suggest standardizing data preprocessing to ensure consistent ff across different regions and developing post-inversion processing techniques that can recover lost information from biased structures. Ultimately, the paper emphasizes the significance of accurately estimating ff when analyzing vector magnetic fields, particularly in relation to photospheric activity. Moreover, the findings support the use of line-of-sight fields as indicators of magnetic energy accumulation before eruptions, given that biased magnetic fields are more unstable. The paper's research focus is relevant to solar physics, particularly in the context of magneto-hydrodynamic theory, where line-of-sight fields serve as a critical indicator of solar flare and erosion precursor analysis. The study's recommendations can be applied to other solar bodies, with which the sun shares similarities in magnetic activity. The Hubbard model's sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations becomes extremely severe as the system's filling factor deviates from half-filling, significantly limiting its study using such methods. Our development of winding-number projection operators addresses this issue. These operators effectively transfer the Monte Carlo sampling from $k$-space to a hybrid $k$-space, allowing us to efficiently study the Hubbard model, especially in inhomogeneously filled systems. By leveraging these projection operators, we can resolve the sign problem and investigate localized states in one-dimensional Hubbard models, both with and without defects, using Monte Carlo simulations. These Monte Carlo simulations match exact results for various correlation functions, even in highly filled systems where the algebraic sign problem is extremely severe. Furthermore, our findings show that despite the sign problem's severity, Monte Carlo simulations can accurately determine the system's filling threshold for realizing localized states and the associated gap width, matching exact results with a high degree of precision. Our approach can be applied to two-dimensional Hubbard models and other strongly correlated electron systems affected by the sign problem. Our research was published in Phys. Rev. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Leveraging these formulas, we determine the homotopy types of boolean complexes for well-known Coxeter groups, including Hanoi groups, braid groups, and Artin groups associated with ternary systems. Moreover, we obtain explicit counts of the spheres within these boolean complexes, allowing us to draw comparisons with alternative counting methods. Our research also includes the properties of a newly introduced Coxeter element, referred to as geometric, which facilitates the extension of our findings to related contexts. We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The study involved using a two-component model to break down elemental patterns into supernovae types and then comparing observed values to predicted values. Differences between the two components were significant, allowing us to determine precise abundances for 15 elements. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, this study leverages data from Sina Weibo, a popular Chinese social media platform, and employs econometric modeling to analyze the dynamics of online rumor propagation in a crisis situation. By accounting for factors such as government response measures, economic fluctuations, lunar events, and online information diffusion patterns, this research seeks to identify the key drivers of online rumor propagation and evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies for containing their spread. The findings provide policy-makers with critical insights for developing targeted interventions to prevent the dissemination of harmful information and promote public health literacy in the face of emerging crises. This study's novel approach to studying online information dynamics is made available through the code shared on an affiliated GitHub page. This research's key results are also presented in a policy brief available on the Pango Policy Institute website. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity, and velocity characteristics of the surrounding stellar system. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distances to the galaxies within the Fornax cluster range from 19 to 24 megaparsecs. Furthermore, a distinct subpopulation of low-luminosity planetary nebulae was discovered, whose frequency significantly increases towards the galaxy cores, and by excluding these low-luminosity sources and reconciling the planetary nebulae masses, the most probable distance to the galaxies within the Fornax cluster has been calculated to be approximately 20 megaparsecs. Notably, this estimate aligns with the values obtained from surface brightness fluctuations analysis of early-type galaxies within the same Fornax cluster, and also corresponds to the expected distance based on the galaxy cluster's Hubble flow velocity. Consequently, a significant improvement in resolving the distance ambiguity associated with the 30 Doradus galaxy has been achieved by applying similar methods, and based on the planetary nebulae frequency distribution, the most probable distance to 30 Doradus has been determined to be approximately 49 kiloparsecs. Additionally, reliable upper and lower limits have been established for this distance estimate. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address this challenge, we present LifeStream, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently, even on commodity hardware. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and specialized big data frameworks by up to 4 times and 2 times respectively, without requiring intricate configuration settings. Additionally, LifeStream is an open-source solution, offering valuable benefits to researchers and practitioners alike, who can leverage and further develop this engine to meet the evolving needs of the medical community. With its impressive performance, user-friendly query language, and open-source nature, LifeStream is an ideal data processing platform for conducting time-series analyses on physiological data across various clinical settings, including both small-scale and large-scale patient data repositories. To demonstrate LifeStream's practical applications, we present StreamMD, a pioneering framework that leverages LifeStream to perform complex medical time-series analyses, thereby paving the way for more accurate medical diagnoses and treatments. To facilitate widespread adoption, the LifeStream code is available on GitHub, along with StreamMD's detailed documentation, examples, and pseudocode for its core components. To facilitate easy deployment, we provide pre-compiled LifeStream binaries for Windows, Linux, and macOS operating systems. To support users in navigating LifeStream's command-line interface, we have developed LifeStream CLI, a user-friendly command-line tool that enables users to effortlessly manage their data streams, queries, and results, even in a headless environment. Ultimately, LifeStream and StreamMD are designed to empower healthcare professionals, researchers, and engineers by equipping them with a high-performance, easy-to-use data processing platform that can conduct time-efficient analyses on vast amounts of physiological data, thereby driving medical progress and improving patient outcomes. To ensure widespread accessibility, LifeStream is available under the highly permissive Apache License 2.0, which allows users to freely leverage, modify, and distribute the engine, as well as incorporate it into various commercial and open-source projects, without incurring any licensing costs or restrictions. We provide explicit definitions for a specific type of curve, namely timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves in higher dimensional spaces, and show that these curves do not exist. Consequently, we redefine this class of curves to include rational surfaces in 4-dimensional space-time, specifically the helicoid and its rotations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a significant subset of these curves corresponds to unique solutions of the Einstein field equations with certain types of topological charges. Additionally, we show that a particular curve, the helicoid, is uniquely associated with the Einstein field equations and a specific topological charge, thereby classifying it among curves with a particular space-time topology. Lastly, we illustrate the geodesics associated with this curve, resulting in a helicoid-shaped singularity and a novel type of knotted black hole with a helicoid-shaped event horizon. This research was inspired by attempting to generalize a specific type of curve, known as Bertrand curve, and exploring its properties in higher dimensional spaces. This led to the discovery of a unique relationship between a particular curve and the Einstein field equations in 4-dimensional space-time. This connection enables the creation of curved space-time systems that yield knotted black hole singularities, providing a possible explanation for the observed knotted nature of singularities in various cosmological contexts. This work paves the way for further study of curve space-time relationships and knotted black hole singularities. This research will be published in the journal General Relativity and Gravitation. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a shift from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction. Additionally, the computation of the Ginzburg parameter suggests that $\kappa \sim 10^{-3}$ in the clean limit, implying that Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is likely an intrinsic type-I superconductor. The theoretical analysis presented in this study provides a framework for understanding the relationship between magnetic properties and electronic band structure in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$. The predictions made here can be tested experimentally and may influence the design of samples with enhanced superconducting properties. The role of disorder on the evolution of magnetic susceptibility in this system is also discussed. The methods employed in this computation can be applied to other materials featuring the $d$-vector order parameter, such as Sr$_2$CuO$_3$ and UTe$_2$. The analysis conducted in this study can be extended to the case of an applied current, which may be relevant for the understanding of edge currents in superconducting materials like Bi$_2$Se$_3$. The relevant Ginzburg-Landau equations were verified to be consistent with earlier research on the subject. The code used for the computations presented in this study is available at https://github.com/ChenGang92/Magnetization-in-Bi2Se3. The theoretical analysis provided in this research complements the experimental findings presented in Ref.\ [\onlinecite{He2022}] and offers predictions for ongoing and future experiments on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with superconducting properties. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a symbol-by-symbol detected signal and a specific differential filter. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through optimized filter design, yielding significant improvements of up to 4 dB in $4\times 10^{-5}$ error probability for various CPM formats. The findings presented can be applied to the transmission of continuous phase modulated signals in diverse channel conditions. The associated simulation and analytical coherent differential detection results serve as references for the error probability improvements achieved. The optimized filter design approach demonstrated is versatile and may be applied to other forms of signal processing applications. The CPM parameter optimization and filter design processes are based on various criteria, including the minimum of mean squared error, the signal-to-noise ratio, and the Bit Error Rate (BER) at specific Doppler shift frequencies. The research focuses on conventional differential detection but offers insights applicable to other forms of differential detection. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our proposed dataset and associated testing framework are designed to facilitate further advancements in artificial intelligence with respect to reasoning about everyday events.  The code and dataset are available online at https://atic.org/.  This repository also contains example generative training code at https://atic.org/generative_experiments.html.  Future developments aimed at refining the semantics of conditional relationships and expanding the scope of ATOMIC to encompass more complex reasoning rules are being made available at https://atic.org/. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation execution and Mid-Circuit Phase Amplification, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of its predictions. To validate the viability of NISQ-HHL, this research develops a mock portfolio-optimization application mirroring the characteristics of real-world instances and employs the IBM Quantum Toolkit to execute NISQ-HHL on multiple NISQ devices, including the Sycamore, Eagle, and System2.0 platforms. Consequently, this study demonstrates the feasibility of employing the HHL quantum algorithm for the sake of portfolio optimization on realistic hardware. These segments follow a specific pattern and have been found to be statistically representative of a linear progression with a consistent mean value of $\frac{n}{2}$ for the first $k_n$ places, where $k_n$ represents an increasing sequence of natural numbers. In particular, as the size of the parking function increases, its initial segments converge to a Gaussian distribution. To illustrate this concept, consider a sequence of random uniform parking functions of successively larger sizes, each with the same number of available spaces, and observe the first $k_n$ designated spots within these parking functions as the size grows. In a recent study, it was observed that the frequency with which the first $k_n$ designated spots match a randomly generated sequence also converges to a Gaussian distribution. In contrast, if the number of available spaces is allowed to increase in proportion to the size of the parking function, its initial segments will consistently reflect a linear progression with a mean value of $\frac{n}{2}$, rather than adhering to a specific statistical distribution. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the paper discussed here, magnetoelectrical transport and the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in particular are investigated for Bi$_2$Se$_3$ layers in contact with a ferromagnetic layer of Gd, and data from transport measurements confirm the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect's impact on Bi$_2$Se$_3$'s near surface layers. Moreover, research reveals the bi-layer system exhibits a large anomalous Hall effect, suggesting potential for the exploration of novel phases with controlled Spin-Orbit Coupling. Moreover, the magnetic proximity effect's influence on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ results in the creation of a magnetic gap above 20K and presents opportunities for exploring magnetic spin elasticity and possible novel magnetic phases with controlled magnetic exchange fields. The bi-layer system's transport properties also demonstrate intriguing temperature and magnetic field dependence, and the corresponding data can be interpreted using a Bismuth-antimony based effective Hamiltonian. The spin-orbit proximity effect's impact on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ near surface layers may also be visualized using a "magnetic potential well" model. The research was conducted using X-ray absorption spectroscopy, transport and magnetoelectrical transport measurements, and was carried out at the IEMR and LURE synchrotron radiation facilities. The theoretical basis for the bi-layer system's properties was developed using the Keldysh diagram technique within the framework of nonequilibrium transport theory. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The code for our work is available online. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep learning models have been successful in enhancing PET images by transferring knowledge from large datasets, but they require access to extensive amounts of training data, presenting a challenge for low-dose and novel PET scans. In response, a innovative framework called Deep Tissue Transfer (DTT) was developed to leverage information from normal-density PET scans for enhanced low-density PET images, without relying on large training sets. DTT utilizes a unique neural network architecture that incorporates multi-resolution encoders and decoders, enabling it to capture both coarse anatomical features and fine details in high-density PET scans, and apply this knowledge to improve low-density PET images. Experiments conducted on various datasets demonstrated the effectiveness of DTT in enhancing PET images at multiple low doses, outperforming traditional deep learning approaches that employ training sets. Specifically, DTT showed notable improvements in image quality, with scores increasing by 19% to 34% in different scenarios, without compromising segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, the framework's efficiency enabled the development of real-time, noise-reduced PET reconstruction algorithms for various sensitive populations, facilitating widespread application of advanced PET imaging techniques. In addition, DTT's versatility allows it to be used for other medical image denoising tasks, beyond PET scans. Resources

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for developing new machine designs that successfully manage beam-RF interactions and overcome the limitations of beam breakup instability. Numerical modeling was conducted utilizing the SAD79 suite of programs, and the proposed theory has been validated using test beams from various energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this study's findings are relevant to other types of particle accelerators affected by beam breakup instability, such as klystrons and radiofrequency guns. By better understanding beam-RF interactions, researchers and engineers can develop more efficient and stable energy recovery linacs, closing the performance gap between simulated and actual machine thresholds. Ultimately, this knowledge can be applied to future energy recovery linacs, potentially unlocking a 5-fold increase in beam current with existing technology. The most promising filling pattern candidates have been identified, and these patterns can be applied to current energy recovery linacs or used as a basis for future machine designs aiming to increase beam current by orders of magnitude. The most effective filling patterns depend on specific machine configurations, but generally speaking, patterns that minimize beam-RF interactions tend to perform best. The energy recovery linac models utilized in this research were modeled after the typical design found in current and planned energy recovery linacs, specifically focusing on the 400 MHz single-pass design. Although the findings of this study are specific to 400 MHz single-pass energy recovery linacs, the underlying beam-RF interaction theory is universally applicable to other particle accelerators affected by beam breakup instability. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes can be effectively analyzed by dividing their outer regions into 'end exclusion zones', whose interactions with each other and with the curved surface can be better understood using simplified models. Based on this concept, we developed a comprehensive theoretical framework for a curved, stretched brush consisting of multiple exclusion zones by mapping its 2D representation onto a 1D linear array, and we applied this approach to study brush behavior on the surfaces of nanoparticles and block copolymer interfaces. By comparing our results with simulation data and experimental observations, we demonstrated the validity and applicability of our theoretical model, and it offers valuable insights for the design of brush-based materials and the fundamental understanding of block copolymer morphology. The results presented in this study provide a solid foundation for further investigation into the complex phenomena associated with curved, stretched brushes, offering a unique perspective on the interplay between brush geometry, solvophilic interactions, and exclusion zone formation. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We show that the minimum identifying sets for the version with an unlimited distance are exactly the metric dimension sets, and that the minimum identifying sets for the version with a limited distance are the same as the minimum dominating sets where the dominating distance is also limited. We also find that the version with a limited distance is at least as difficult as the version with an unlimited distance, and that both versions of the problem are hard, requiring time to find the minimum identifying sets that is exponential with the square of the number of vertices in the graph. We provide this with an example of a specific graph G that has a large metric dimension and thus a large minimum identifying set when the distance is unlimited, but a very small minimum identifying set when the distance is limited to two steps. We conclude by discussing some possible applications of this problem. We also include some test data for a program that can find minimum identifying sets of a graph with limited distance. We hope this will be useful for researchers who want to examine larger graphs. We further note that the version of this problem with an unlimited distance is equivalent to the problem of finding the minimum metric dimension of a graph, and thus a subset of the parameters that we tested have been previously reported by others in the field of graph theory. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Additionally, it facilitates a more precise determination of the spectrum of extremely bright sources, as it deconvolves the Comptonization process used in image reconstruction. Consequently, this multifaceted approach has substantial implications for the analysis of future space telescopes, like the Chaser satellite, with wide-field-of-view instruments, which will generate vast amounts of data in the same manner as the Fermi Telescope. To this end, the code has been made publicly available to facilitate widespread adoption within the astronomical community. To validate the dictionary learning approach, a specialized simulation was utilized, comprising 2,000 images with target extractions similar to real data, with results showing that the algorithm effectively retrieves original images, even when subject to Comptonization "scrambling". Furthermore, a comparative study was conducted versus the commonly employed Fermi Surface Brightness Level (SBLL) analysis method, which yielded equivalent source detection sensitivities but superior resolution, along with improved recovery of complex source shapes, extended structures, and the galactic plane. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential negative labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that can be integrated into existing GAN training methods to produce high-quality multi-label data.  Experimental findings demonstrate that using single-to-multi-label data generated in this way can significantly enhance the performance of conditions that are not easily distinguished, condition several object recognition tasks, and contribute to innovative research on unsupervised clustering based on generative models. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation by showing it observables can be viewed as a functor from the concrete setting of state representations to the more abstract setting of C*-algebras, with the functors behaving in a coherent manner under equivalence transformations. This coherent behavior is represented by a natural transformation that makes the GNS construction a kind of inverse process, thereby creating a natural isomorphism between the original algebra and the one obtained via GNS construction from its state representation. We also establish that this process is compatible with the notion of coarse-graining, or reduction of states, by finding that the GNS construction of a state reduced via partial trace is naturally isomorphic to the reduced algebra of the original state. As a result, we obtain the GNS construction as a natural process to couple any theory of quantum physics with its classical counterpart. This connection allows us to interpret the GNS construction as generating quasilocal quantum theories from their global counterparts, demonstrating that quasilocal theories are a natural extension of local ones. We also explore the relationship between quasilocal theories and their extension to global ones, discovering that not all global theories can be obtained from their corresponding quasilocal versions, but those that can are classified as locally accessible. It is proposed that a link exists between this paradox and the "radiative mode" black hole accretion, which can cause a decline in hard X-ray emissions. Based on this hypothesis, a new monitor for gamma-rays has been established using the Fermi Large Area Telescope and the Swift X-ray Telescope, focused on the most powerful radio galaxies that exhibit soft X-ray characteristics. These sources were observed for 10 years, but no gamma-ray signal was detected from any of them, confirming the initial expectations by a margin of 99.99%. The most plausible explanation for this non-detection is the prevalence of radiative mode accretion, which can lead to the emission of high-energy gamma-rays as observed in blazars. The absence of gamma-ray emission in low-luminosity black holes may also provide a possible explanation for the observed deficit of gamma-ray sources. The availability of long-term hard X-ray monitoring allows for the verification of the prevalence of radiative mode accretion, which can lead to the formation of low-energy gamma-rays within the jets of these sources, as observed in the case of M87*. The study of radio galaxies that emit X-rays may offer a unique means of discovering these elusive gamma-ray sources and understanding the dependence of accretion modes on black hole mass. The energy of these gamma-rays is consistent with the prevalence of radiative mode accretion, but the limited observation period may not be sufficient to confirm this finding. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study employs a device-independent approach using a discriminative neural network to distinguish normal and pathological sounds based on a broad spectrum of features extracted from short-duration recordings.  A large dataset of 4,020 recordings (2,020 training, 500 validation, and 1,490 testing recordings) was collected from various sources, comprising 1,440 pathological and 2,580 normal recordings, each 2.5 seconds long.  Experimental results showed that the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 93.1% in differentiating normal and pathological sounds, surpassing the performance of conventional machine learning classifiers and comparing favorably to the outcomes of other deep learning models.  The effectiveness of the model was further validated through the calculation of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PR), in addition to an analysis of the feature importance of the discriminative neural network. Successful smart healthcare relies on effectively utilizing this data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, a huge volume of generated data creates significant processing difficulties, and secondly, personalization is necessary to tailor healthcare solutions to individual users. A subsequent section demonstrates the method's effectiveness using a simulated dataset and an illustrative policy case study. The results show that this approach yields better data reduction ratios and personalized targeting accuracy compared to existing methods. The research provides a theoretical framework along with policy-relevant applications for wearable technology usage in healthcare. This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations. Furthermore, the potential skewness and kurtosis optimization pitfalls are demonstrated numerically, followed by a stochastic volatility model application. The results show that the hedge fund returns' non-normal characteristics pose significant challenges for optimization algorithms, yet the SV model reveals that some portfolios can consistently achieve desired skewness and kurtosis levels. Ultimately, the study advocates for a robust perspective on portfolio optimization, emphasizing the necessity of considering the interplay between returns' moments and fundamental risk management. Suggested future research directions include investigating robust optimization methods, examining the portfolio performance impact of various moment targets, and exploring the applicability of machine learning techniques. In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. Our findings provide statistical insights into the effectiveness of these methods. This research may serve as a foundation for further expansion of our prototype, enabling real-time application processing. We address a complex control issue with multiple stages, guided by an augmented formulation. This problem involves switching controls and represents a systematic expansion of an existing problem that assumes a single stage and no control discontinuities, as first addressed by the authors in their prior work, where they provided a direct method to determine optimal cost functions, albeit noted as fragmented due to the presence of regime changes. To tackle this challenge, we employ a staged perspective and an augmented formulation to reframe the original problem, ultimately leading to a system of nonlinear equations whose solution yields the desired optimal cost function, unaffected by the presence of regime changes. This extension enables us to control and optimize multiple stages with varying durations, as well as stages with different start and end points, all within a single framework. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we present numerical results obtained using a nonlinear least squares method, applied to a synthetic data set. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical utility of this method by applying it to a real-world problem involving the control of a helicopter in hover, where the objective is to minimize roll and pitch oscillations while adhering to specific constraints, and to evaluate the system's robustness in the presence of additive noise. To achieve this, we modify the helicopter's dynamics model to incorporate stochastic terms and solve a stochastic control problem, for which we use a direct method to determine the optimal cost function, necessary for subsequent Monte Carlo simulations. The effectiveness of this method is evident when applying it to a helicopter control scenario, where the optimal cost function enables robust control solutions to be found through multiple Monte Carlo simulations, thereby validating the helicopter control system design against a range of operating conditions. Systematic expansions of the original problem, including multiple stages with varying durations and different start and end points, are also considered, along with a control problem involving a helicopter in hover, for which we present numerical results using a nonlinear least squares method and validate the system against a range of operating conditions using a direct method for a stochastic control problem. To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks are created in pairs with different charges, behaving in a way that is highly distinctive at the particle level and can be verified with certain colliders. Using the ATLAS and CMS experiments' current capabilities, our study demonstrates how to utilize asymmetric production in the 13 TeV proton-proton collider to create leptoquarks of various types, specifically second-generation leptoquarks, Third-generation leptoquarks, and scalar leptoquarks. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Additionally, this result can be used to demonstrate that the ASEP system, initialized with a step function, will eventually reach a stationary state where the particle velocity follows a uniform probability distribution over the interval $[-1,1]$, thus confirming a key aspect of its expected stationary state. Furthermore, this research provides specific insights into the ASEP speed process and enables us to apply its properties in addressing both of the system's conjectures mentioned above. It is worth noting that the ASEP system's behavior as time approaches infinity is found to be similar to that observed in TASEP, with the notable difference being the eventual stationary state's characteristics. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic, focusing on epidemic, disease, and network models. Initially, key characteristics of traditional Kermack-McKendrick models are explained, followed by a comprehensive review of recent model developments, including differential equation-based models, discrete models, differential equation-based models with time lags, optimal control models, and network models. A significant section is dedicated to applications of these models, such as forecasting, early warning systems, policy-making, control strategies, and understanding epidemic resilience. Furthermore, discussions surround statistical analysis, notable outbreaks, specific diseases, and mathematical contributions, including model-based insights into pandemic dynamics, analysis, numerical methods, and various extensions. By synthesizing this knowledge, researchers aim to provide valuable insights for policymakers, healthcare professionals, and the general public, as well as identify areas for future work and potential research directions. This review is an extension of previous work, with a focus on models developed in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, and is intended to contribute to the ongoing effort of addressing global health challenges through mathematical modeling. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in both systems. Our research uncovered both magnetically unstable conditions as well as the minimum number of atoms required for oscillatory behavior in both scenarios. In addition, we simulated numerically the development of magnetically unstable conditions in both scenarios using a BEC of $^{87}$Rb atoms. Our theoretical findings are relevant to experimental setups involving atoms such as $^{1}$H, $^{7}$Li, $^{23}$Na, and $^{85,87}$Rb. Our research was motivated by recent atom-molecule interconversion experiments conducted with BEC of $^{87}$Rb spin-1 atoms. Our study provides a detailed examination of initial conditions required for stable creation of atom-molecule pairs, in addition to theoretical analysis of magnetic instability in a system with one spin unit, which may find applications in the study of dyonic BECs, atomic condensates with non-Abelian statistics, and magnetic field effects on BECs. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects based on the connections between their corresponding genomic loci. Unlike existing approaches, this design allows for efficient management of large datasets, particularly with regard to updating specific entries, which becomes increasingly time-consuming as data size grows exponentially in previous methods due to closure under concatenation. Building upon this architecture's core properties, we create a specialized genetic algorithm capable of modifying specific entries while avoiding unnecessary reencoding of unrelated data objects, effectively minimizing storage overhaul when updating small portions of the dataset. Our results demonstrate improved performance when compared to state-of-the-art DNA-storage solutions, both in terms of computation time and storage efficiency, according to various evaluation metrics including entry update time, total reencoding time, and overall storage usage. Leveraging Amazon Openthrift binary serialization, we successfully encode and store a real-world dataset comprising 130 objects across approximately 13MB of sequence space, on top of an initial 100MB placeholder genome. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuangdalin/DNA-storage, along with an interactive online demo at https://kuangdalin.github.io/DNA-storage/. Our findings also highlight the significance of selecting appropriate binary serialization formats to balance size and readability, paving the way for further exploration in the field of DNA-based data storage. Our research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under grant number 62172284. Knowles-Dix-Hansen type inequality was utilized to derive key performance bounds in our study. Our project was inspired by the DNA storage challenge organized by Microsoft Corporation and the recent work published by Guo et al. Our team would like to express their gratitude to Dr. Yansong Wu for his valuable input and to the students who contributed to the project, including Yifan Song, Yujie Liu, and Yuhao Li. Precise river flow velocity predictions are highly influential in preventing flooding disasters and protecting riverine ecosystems. Traditionally, these predictions are generated using complex numerical solvers, which, despite advancements, are still limited by the quality of their solutions, particularly when dealing with high-capacity datasets. In contrast, machine learning algorithms offer faster and more accurate predictions, making them an attractive alternative. However, previous attempts to apply these algorithms for predicting river flow velocities using advanced deep learning models have been unsuccessful due to overfitting. In response, this study proposes a novel, simple approach using a linear regression model that leverages an innovative technique called graph convolution neural networks to enhance the accuracy of predictions by accounting for spatial relationships among river nodes. In addition, this study presents a new pseudo-Sarimal model to improve the performance of linear regression by incorporating additional information from water flow dynamics. The proposed method is put to practical use in predicting flow velocities at specific river points in Hanoi, Vietnam, based on historical data from the past five years. The results show that this approach yields superior predictions when compared to traditional methods, demonstrating its potential value in real-world river flow velocity prediction applications. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, our project presents Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), the first comprehensive robot navigation platform designed to assess robots' ability to navigate multiple, dynamically changing environments, and learn from experience applying what they've learned in one context to benefit others. L2Explorer offers multiple variants to cater to diverse, emerging challenges in lifelong learning, and features several innovative features, including varied scene configurations, moving obstacles, unexpected events, and multiple learning scenarios, all fully operational via a user-friendly web interface that allows effortless experiment management, precise control, and data analysis. By contributing a distinctive, publicly accessible dataset in addition to L2Explorer itself, we aim to facilitate meaningful advancements in lifelong learning robotics through the free availability of both the software and associated research data. The L2Explorer framework, alongside its affiliated repository containing educational materials, guidance on usage, and technical details, is accessible online at the following URL: https://lifelonglearningexplorer.org/. To foster collaboration and knowledge sharing within the robotics community, we also invite participants to engage with L2Explorer through a dedicated forum portal located at the following URL: https://forum.lifelonglearningexplorer.org/. System specifications for L2Explorer are as follows: the project requires Ubuntu 20.04 LTS operating system, Simulation Environment version 2021.2.0 or later, Navigation System version 2.1.0 or later, and Python 3.8 or later. To replicate the experiments and gain access to associated data, register on the official website at the following URL: https://register.lifelonglearningexplorer.org/. Experimental findings are already included in a pre-print version of a paper that can be accessed through the following URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11664. Future developments related to L2Explorer are outlined in the appendix section of the aforementioned pre-print version. To contact the project team, send an email to the following address: lifelonglearningexplorer@googlegroups.com. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Leveraging this research, future studies can build upon existing knowledge by exploring extensions, similar process mining tasks, and various process representations. Our code and test dataset are accessible at https://github.com/zhongju-li/process-mining.

This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. Specifically, it focuses on explaining the relationship between generalized Hodge structures and Deligne's conjectural theory of motives, with the aim of establishing that the space of generalized Hodge structures, subject to certain conditions, is isomorphic to a specific subspace of the motive space. This result has implications for the compactification of moduli spaces, offering a perspective through the lens of Geometric Hodge Theory and Motivic Hodge Theory. Building on the work of many mathematicians, this exposition leverages the findings of Kerr, Miller, and Thomas to extend their research and illustrate the principles behind functors that produce motives, as seen in the studies of Andre, Deligne, Kerr, Miller, and Murre. Ultimately, this exploration sheds light on the motives underlying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties and related geometric inferences. This work is an expansion of talks delivered at the 2017 CRM-Fields summer school on Geometric Hodge Theory and its interactive aspects with Algebraic Geometry. It is intended for a broad audience of mathematicians interested in the connections between Hodge theory, algebraic geometry, and number theory. S. If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. Our investigation reveals that the issue stems from the uneven distribution of positive and negative samples. To address this imbalance, we integrate a Positive Sample Mining module to enhance the quality of negative samples by removing insignificant relationships. Our improvements are also applicable to other widely used datasets, where our model surpasses the current state-of-the-art in the MS COC sub-task of VRD and the AI21 School of VRD challenge dataset. A comprehensive analysis of spectroscopic observations from the VLT is presented, focusing on measurements of core and surface rotation rates in low-mass stars undergoing subgiant stages.  By applying the venous-ejecta model to combine measurements from two spectroscopic methods, core rotation rates were determined for 15 stars from a previously studied sample of 21 low-mass giants.  The analysis revealed evidence for differential rotation within these stars, with a calculated omega1 value of 1.43 +/- 0.04 cycles per day.  This result is consistent with predictions made by theoretical models of stellar evolution, and may indicate that low-mass stars retain a faster core rotation rate from their pre-main sequence stage.  However, more detailed comparison also suggests a possible slight slowdown of core rotation, which could be caused by an incorrect assumption in the venous-ejecta model or actual deceleration of core rotation during the subgiant stage.  Further investigation is necessary to determine the source of this possible phenomenon.  The calculated core rotation rates are coupled with existing data to construct a diagram plotting core rotation against the position of the stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.  This diagram provides visual evidence for a connection between core rotation and stellar evolution, specifically the occurrence of radial oscillations in low-mass stars.  A notable absence of these oscillations in stars with core rotation rates above 1.5 cycles per day is observed, and may indicate a threshold above which differential rotation becomes unstable and leads to radial enrichment, and as a result, the cessation of radial oscillations.  This connection could be further explored with additional data from space telescopes, and may also be relevant to understanding planetary interaction with stars in the subgiant stage.  This research was conducted as part of the PAST project, which aims to study pre-main sequence and low-mass stellar evolution using spectroscopic and direct imaging techniques.  The sample analyzed in this study was chosen from the PAST project database based on suitable conditions, and consists of 21 low-mass stars with different rotation rates, and for which multiple observations are available.  These conditions include: the presence of surface rotation-induced spectroscopic broadening, the absence of any significant chemical anomalies, and the position of the stars in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, specifically within the subgiant stage.  The methodology used to analyze the data included the application of the venous-ejecta model, which combines the results of two methods for measuring core rotation rates

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining an existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-task neural sequence learning approach that can detect false information on unexpected events with limited information, without the need for retraining the model. This method leverages the knowledge gained from detecting false information on similar events with abundant data, by conducting neural sequence learning on the combined text of these events. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets confirmed the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating its ability to accurately detect false information on unexpected events with a high degree of success. Specifically, our proposed method showed a 12% improvement in the detection of false information compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques on the IFLC2019 dataset, and a 15% improvement on the FCTC2020 dataset. In addition to the detection of false information, our approach also achieved a 20% increase in the accuracy of news categorization on unexpected events, and a 10% boost in the detection of hate speech on social media, according to the FCTC2020 dataset standards. In the case of the IFLC2019 dataset, our method exhibited a 10% improvement in this regard. Our code is available online at https://github.com/amarjadiya/MDTNS at no cost. In order to foster further advancement in the field, we are making publicly available pre-trained models on the combined text of 13 events with vast amounts of labeled data, which can be utilized as base models for the detection of false information on unexpected events with limited information, at no expense. In particular, these models can be obtained from https://github.com/amarjadiya/MDTNS/tree/main/pretrained_models. In order to promote progress in the field and based on environmental considerations, our code and pre-trained models are available for free.
