To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach also provides valuable insights into the knowledge sources deemed necessary for answering specific questions. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. To address this issue, we consider a fixed budget for the number of iterations and node-server communications. Given this constraint, we aim to develop a Federated Learning algorithm that enables accurate model predictions based on initial data observations. Building on the FedProx framework, we propose a novel method called Distributed Mirror Descent (DMD), tailored for smooth and unheterogeneous data distributions across nodes. We prove that DMD complies with the desired communication budget and provides an accurate model prediction, with performance guaranteed by a $O(1/\sqrt{B})$ convergence rate. To demonstrate the efficacy of DMD, we conduct numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world data sets. Additionally, we apply DMD to a prominent classification problem, achieving notable improvements over existing algorithms. With its versatility, DMD can be effectively used in various graph-structured learning scenarios. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates North Carolina saved $1,441 per defendant on average or $13 million annually by requiring mental health treatment as part of their sentence.  A second analysis that takes into account the total costs associated with the justice system finds that providing mental health treatment as part of a sentence can lead to cost savings within the three-year timeframe and large savings in the long term.  A descriptive breakdown of the data shows that among those who committed a crime again, those who received mental health treatment were more likely to commit a new crime within the first year of their original sentence but those who didn't commit a new crime within that year had a very low chance of committing a crime in the following two years.  An analysis of factors associated with within one-year and three-year recidivism rates reveals that receiving mental health treatment reduces the likelihood of committing a crime again within one year by 14 percent or 6.5 percentage points and three years by 12 percent or 4.5 percentage points.  It also finds that younger offenders and those with more severe charges are more likely to commit a crime again within the three-year timeframe and that offenders who were given mental health treatment as part of their sentence but didn't complete it have a higher chance of committing a crime again within the three-year timeframe than those who did complete it.  Finally, it finds that among those who committed a crime again, receiving mental health treatment as part of their original sentence decreases the likelihood of committing a new crime that results in incarceration by 21 percent or 11 percentage points within the three-year timeframe.  An examination of the relationship between the distance from the original conviction date and the likelihood of committing a crime again shows that the likelihood of committing a crime again within the three-year timeframe is lowest

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation, without relying on paired data. The proposed strategy uses a combination of cyclic consistency and inter-domain regularization to train a model on partially annotated images. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the semi-supervised segmentation of MRI scans, using a publicly available dataset with limited annotation. Compared to supernet-based methods, the proposed regularizer achieves comparable performance using significantly less annotated data, and the results show a significant improvement over the baseline model. The proposed technique's strengths and limitations are further highlighted through the conduct of additional experiments. The code for this research is available online. The utility of the regularizer in other medical imaging tasks and scenarios is also explored. The proposed regularizer is applicable to other publicly available medical image datasets, and the feasibility of extending it to real-world clinical settings is discussed. The future directions for improving the technique are identified, including the incorporation of spatial consistency and contrastive learning regularization. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is put to the test
using simulations of aluminum atoms undergoing thermal fluctuations, comparisons
with experimental atomic disorder measurements, and evaluations of its effect
on material properties, specifically focusing on the solid-liquid phase boundary
where disorder has the most significant impact. Our study demonstrates how our
approach can be utilized to extract critical information from simulations and
experiments, and highlights the potential applications in the discovery of new
materials and understanding material phase transitions. To facilitate reproduction
of results and future developments, our code is openly available at https://github.com/AtomAI/GNN-atomic-disorder.

2.5 fs, resulting in 100,000 structures per temperature range. To account for
thermal fluctuations, we ran ten independent simulations at each temperature.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The approach is applicable to scenarios with multiple levels of mixing distributions. The software used for the examples is available online. The method presented in this work has been used in the research of the author and has been published separately, see Xie (2017, 2018, 2019). The thesis was completed in 2016. The primary research component of this thesis is independent from the joint work with the thesis supervisor, whereas the methodological development was heavily influenced by the supervisor. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates consistent data preprocessing across 13 diverse educational datasets and provides predictive performance assessments on multiple evaluation metrics for 12 prominent deep learning knowledge tracing models. Empirical studies conducted using PyKT reveal model performance inconsistencies and provide valuable insights into effective knowledge graph construction. These findings can guide practitioners in selecting suitable models and developing more effective knowledge graph-based representations to enhance student performance predictions. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, it is shown that if a manifold $M$ lacks compact components, then any $H^2(M)$ function can be expressed as the image of a harmonic function from $C^\infty(M)$. The underlying principles are then utilized to prove the solvability of the Helmholtz equation for $L^2$ Sobolev spaces on arbitrary manifolds. The examination is completed by discussing the concepts of partial elliptic operators and their corresponding images, as well as exploring their implications for the Helmholtz decomposition of specific spaces of functions. The research is complemented by an overview of its connections to an earlier study focused on a different type of decomposition. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical applications of this algorithm in realistic settings. The code for the FedBuff algorithm is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/lingostatus/FedBuff. The code has been successfully used in submitting algorithms to competitions hosted on the AICrowd platform, specifically the FFL2021 challenge organized by Huawei. The algorithm's performance was ranked second among 14 submissions, surpassing several submissions utilizing traditional federated learning methods. The code can be utilized for other supervised learning tasks, such as multiclassification problems. The research underlying the FedBuff algorithm has been published in a study available on the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.12879. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. This study explores the utilization of a trained English neural network for Czech ASR, employing an intermediate alphabet with simplified diacritic notation. The results indicate a significant reduction of overfitting when using this approach, thus our hypothesis is confirmed that the method is effective in reducing neural network complexity, thereby beneficial for small-scale Czech data sets. Furthermore, the research reveals that the technique can be beneficial for larger data sets, albeit to a lesser extent. A thorough examination of various preprocessing methods for Czech text data is also conducted, revealing that the application of an intermediate alphabet yields the most notable effects. This implies that acoustic feature extraction could be another bottleneck for deep neural networks in ASR systems. The optimal preprocessing method is presented, along with a comparative analysis of the technique for different data sets. The research further delves into the utilization of the approach for low-resource languages that employ non-Latin scripts, such as Slovak and Czech, employing an extended version of the intermediate alphabet, and the results are compared to those obtained with the original alphabet. The findings suggest that the method can be effective for these languages as well, albeit requiring further investigation. The study also compares the results with those reported for German ASR, which is a higher-resource language than Czech. The code and trained models are available online for the benefit of the research community. The research is an initial step towards developing neural network models for languages with non-Latin scripts, and it paves the way for future work aimed at training models directly on such data sets. The research also highlights the importance of alphabet preprocessing methods on the performance of deep neural networks in ASR systems. The findings encourage further investigation into the utilization of transfer learning for ASR systems in languages with non-Latin scripts, and the development of new alphabet preprocessing methods that are more effective and do not rely on the use of intermediate alphabets. The code and models are available at https://github.com/michalmalewski/tt2phn_czech. The research was supported by the Czech Technical University in Prague, and the models can be accessed at https://www.fifthwave.cz/asr-cz-en. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA, a new algorithm for offline data.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and our findings show that both variants excel over the standard TD learning in various underwater navigation scenarios.  Our code is available online at https://github.com/zhongyuyu/SPGP-SARSA.  Future research will concentrate on integrating our method with other sampling strategies and evaluating its performance in other marine environments.  As underwater robots become more precise and their computing power grows, our algorithm is poised to become increasingly efficient.  Our findings also suggest potential applications to other challenging-to-reach environments, such as pipeline inspection.  Our approach can be used with any state-function learning method by replacing standard TD learning with SPGP-TD.  As such, our method provides a versatile framework for value-function learning in challenging-to-reach environments. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be extended to the two-fluid scenario, providing a basis for classifying solutions. Specifically, two-fluid versions of the Jaramilac-Novikov solution and the Fikman solution are derived, along with a one-fluid solution as a two-fluid solution. The employed method allows for the direct construction of solutions from their four-potentials, bypassing the need for metric reconstruction. The anisotropic nature of the solutions is demonstrated through pressure anisotropy equations. The mass-radius relationships for the Jaramilac-Novikov solution and the Fikman solution are also obtained as well as the compactness bounds for these solutions. The employed method's versatility is further illustrated by deriving the Einstein field equations directly from the four-potential approach, offering an alternative to the direct resolution method for obtaining solutions. The relevance of the four-potential approach to the covariant semi-tetrad method is confirmed by the derived four-potential components. The method's applicability to dynamic and asymmetric scenarios is discussed. The employed four-potential components can be further used to describe dynamic and asymmetric scenarios, potentially through the application of the de Donder-Weyl covariant semi-tetrad method, which would result in a system of nonlinear partial differential equations. The four-potential components also allow for the description of the energy-momentum tensor's conservation, the Bianchi identity, and the relationship between the curvature and the four-potential. The method's limitations are discussed in the context of singularities and the need for refined metrics in certain solution cases. The employed four-potential approach is shown to be equivalent to the direct resolution method for single-fluid solutions. The method's validity is confirmed by applying it to known solutions and comparing the obtained results with existing literature. The employed four-potential components can be written in a form that is manifestly consistent with the assumptions of static and spherical symmetry. The method's applicability to the two-fluid case is discussed in the context of two-fluid models with specific pressure relationships, such as the radiation-dominated case and the stiff fluid limit

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that can be applied to impoverished target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that our approach outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning method by a 0.50 F score on average and enables domain adaptation with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our approach compares favorably to strong sentence-level retargetting baselines in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with average scores of 17.32, 63.19 and 50.30 for English, Dutch and German respectively. However, our performance may be improved by integrating retargetting technology. The proposed method's code has been made available online at the WMT 2023 workshop website.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition, as well as being maximal with respect to a specific partial order, as initially observed by Series. Additionally, we established that for any number of agents greater than one, no mechanism exists that, regardless of the situation, produces equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared values as input, for the case of allocating non-divisible goods fair up any good. Moreover, we explored extensions of the Plaut and Roughgarden method to the allocation of divisible goods, as well as a broader class of mechanisms that are induced by rules of order, for which we established that the corresponding equilibria are maximal with respect to a specific partial order, as well as being fair with respect to a particular fairness condition known as maximin share fairness. Lastly, we discussed a natural extension of the Plaut and Roughgarden method that, for any number of agents, generates allocations that are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a particular maximin share fairness condition for a specific subclass of valuation functions. Furthermore, we established that for the case of two agents, no mechanism exists that, regardless of the situation, produces equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared values as input,

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 may be linked to its interaction history, given the presence of a prominent, low surface brightness spiral arm that could indicate past interactions with massive galaxies. The distinct star formation patterns in UGC 8839 might also result from a rare, self-regulating feedback mechanism, given the presence of massive black holes in the galaxy, inferred by broad HII region line profiles and the presence of a central, low-luminosity nucleus. The study of UGC 8839 offers valuable insights into the extreme, off-axis star formation observed in certain low surface brightness spiral galaxies, and highlights the significance of considering the interplay between baryonic and dark matter in understanding their evolution. The research is further supported by numerical simulations demonstrating how a unique feedback loop, fueled by massive black holes, can create stable, far-reaching gas flows, resulting in the formation of distant HII regions. The study suggests that such a mechanism could account for the extreme star formation in UGC 8839 and may represent a distinct pathway in galaxy evolution, with potential implications for the understanding of low surface brightness spiral galaxies and the role of dark matter in their development. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although these predictions align with many of our observations, some deviations are also observed, particularly with regard to the impact of the quark mass. Our data can be represented by an extended version of the standard chiral perturbation theory framework, with additional terms that account for the effects of the intermediate energy scale on the behavior of quark currents within the pion. Our research provides insights into the fundamental interactions governing quark currents within hadrons and establishes a crucial link between lattice QCD simulations and the chiral effective theory used to describe the behavior of hadrons at the quark level. Our specific findings will contribute to the development of an extended chiral perturbation theory framework capable of accurately predicting the behavior of quark currents within mesons in the non-perturbative regime of QCD. Our comprehensive dataset of correlation functions will be made available to the community, enabling further analysis and comparison with results obtained using other theoretical approaches. Our research was conducted using the ILC ensemble ILC50a1024k at a lattice spacing of approximately 0.0185 au, corresponding to a physical pion mass of approximately 310 MeV. Our findings were validated for quark masses in the range 0.036 to 0.288 au, and our effective theory predictions were validated for momentum ranges from 4 to 20 GeV au-1. Our research consisted of simulating 12,288 lattice configurations with a time interval of 0.04 au between each configuration. Our pion correlation function signals had a physical extent of approximately 7 au. Our research was conducted on a 16^3 96 lattice. Our quark current correlation function data can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.79140/ARXAQUE/1. mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed $L_\mathrm{acc}$ over time is complicated
due to uncertainty about when and how mass accretion rates change during
stellar formation, specifically during the T Tauri stage.  In this work, we
investigate how $L_\mathrm{acc}$ is affected by several factors, including
disk evaporating objects, mass accretion rates, X-ray emissions, and
turbulence, using high-resolution simulations of stars and protoplanetary disks.
By analyzing these simulations, we found that $L_\mathrm{acc}$ is directly
related to $ \dot{M}$ over a certain range, but also exhibits a more complex
behavior influenced by other processes, such as the dissipation of
magnetohydrodynamic waves, the strength of turbulence, and the mass of the
star.  By comparing these results with observed $L_\mathrm{acc}$ values, we
determined that $ \dot{M}$ during the T Tauri stage is approximately $10^{-8}$
Solar masses per year.  Additionally, we found that the relationship between
$ \dot{M}$ and $L_\mathrm{acc}$ changes during the T Tauri stage, which has
implications for using $L_\mathrm{acc}$ as a proxy for $ \dot{M}$ in the past
and future.  Finally, we discuss the limitations of this approach when
considering future missions with enhanced sensitivity to $L_\mathrm{acc}$.  By
analyzing the SFR of nearby star-forming regions, we calculated the past
and future $ \dot{M}$ for low-mass stars in these regions, which can be used
to predict the number of T Tauri stars with certain $L_\mathrm{acc}$ values
in the past and future.  By doing this for existing and future transition
 disk detection limits, we can anticipate the discovery of previously
 undetected T Tauri stars with certain mass accretion rates in the past and
 future.  Specifically, we found that many T Tauri stars with $ \dot{M} \geq

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The code and models are available for public use.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our 2D and 3D models achieved better Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) and lower surface distance (SD) values compared to 2D and 3D conventional methods. Moreover, our 2D and 3D models showed increased robustness when applied to poorly registered pairs of images. Additionally, our 2D model yielded a 2.5-fold increase in capture range when applied to simulated data. Lastly, our 2D and 3D models successfully registered real megavoltage images of abdominopelvic organs, albeit with some limitations when it came to surface alignment. Nonetheless, both models successfully aligned surfaces near organs, with notable surface alignment near the lungs in the 2D model. Our Convolutional Neural Network-based model exhibits promising performance for registering real megavoltage images, albeit with scope for further improvement, primarily with regards to capturing soft tissue surface information. Nonetheless, our findings provide a solid foundation for future enhancements, such as integrating gradient information and utilizing better loss functions, with potential applications in radiotherapy, among others. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/charlesshy/MV-registration.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. Utilizing the elaborate setup proposed by Einstein, we investigate the instantaneous impact generated by the measurement of one particle on another, distant particle, with the aid of decoherent quantum trajectories and continuous measurement theory. Our analysis highlights the distinct patterns of instantaneous effects resulting from various initial conditions and the boundary between local and non-local instantaneous influences. Ultimately, we establish a connection between these findings and the notion of causal loops predicted by quantum mechanics, with implications for understanding the limits of local reality. With the aid of an analogy involving a hierarchical network, we clarify how the development of causal loops, fueled by the measurement process, can lead to the degradation of quantum non-locality and the emergence of particle decay patterns observable in experiments. With this comprehensive analysis, we provide a concrete illustration of the intricate relationship between the conceptual frameworks of quantum non-locality, causality, and reality. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. This includes a detailed examination of FL algorithms, security protocols, and BC-based architectures for various IoVs applications, as well as an assessment of the computational costs associated with these solutions. This review is further supplemented by an illustrative example and graphical analysis of the most pertinent performance indicators for SEBC-FLIoV protocols. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning each component a precoder, and directs the mobile terminal to provide feedback on the GMM components with the highest likelihood, thereby indicating the relevant precoders. This approach yields improved performance over traditional methods, offering reduced feedback load without significant loss in estimation accuracy, and is suitable for scenarios with limited channel feedback. Numerical data demonstrates improved system performance metrics, including SINR and throughput, when utilizing the novel codebook feedback scheme. Algebraic expressions facilitating practical implementation are provided, along with suggestions for optimizing GMM characteristics for optimal system performance. System parameters such as GMM size, codebook size, and target SINR significantly influence performance and feedback load, and various scenarios are presented to illustrate practical applications. A hypothetical outdoor scenario is simulated to evaluate the proposed method, showing that GMM-based codebooks can yield a 15% increase in feedback load, but with reduced impact on performance, whereas in a more realistic indoor environment, the increase in feedback load is more pronounced, at 50%, but the proposed method still offers improved system performance. Algebraic expressions facilitate codebook design based on specific system requirements, and guidelines for optimizing GMM characteristics for optimal system performance are presented, including that the codebook size should be 4 times the GMM size for optimal performance, and that GMM characteristics should be tailored to the local environment, with recommendations for both outdoor and indoor scenarios, including suggested GMM sizes of 16 and 64 respectively. A theoretical analysis of system performance is conducted using algebraic expressions, and compared to existing methods, the novel approach offers a 20% increase in feedback load but with a 10% improvement in SINR and a 5% increase in throughput. A simulation of a time-division duplex system with limited channel feedback shows that the proposed codebook design approach yields a 10% increase in feedback load but with a 15% improvement in SINR and a 10% increase in throughput, and that the codebook size should be 4 times the GMM size for optimal performance, and that GMM characteristics should be tailored to the local environment, with recommendations for both outdoor and indoor scenarios, including suggested GMM sizes of 16 and 64 respectively. Quantum systems exhibit intriguing behavior at their boundaries, and research has focused on two-dimensional robust crosscurrents driven by three-dimensional symmetry protection. Our study explores the robustness of these currents in three-dimensional lattice systems, specifically with impurities present, and reveals that stability is ensured when interactions between particles are weak and near their non-interacting form, where the energy spectrum exhibits Dirac-like behavior. Using an example based on a Hofstadter model, we demonstrate the robustness of helical currents against disorder and damping in both two-dimensional planes and in three-dimensional bulk regions. Moreover, our findings indicate that edge currents in three-dimensional systems can persist locally, even in the presence of strong interactions, and that these currents can arise even in systems without an apparent helical character. Our approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the robustness of these currents and sheds light on distinct features of boundary and bulk regions. The research was conducted without knowledge of a prior related study published in Science, due to the abstract knowledge cutoff date.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7 times the current Milky Way mass in nuclear star clusters at redshift zero should have Population III binary remnants formed during the early universe. These clusters should be able to produce supercircularization events with total masses between 10 and 100 solar masses at rates of 0.03 to 0.3 per century. Additionally, our predictions indicate that nuclear star clusters at redshift greater than 0 should be capable of producing massive star mergers at rates of 10 to 100 per year. Our model suggests that the most massive of these events, with total masses between 50 and 130 solar masses, should primarily occur in nuclear star clusters at redshift greater than 0. Our predictions are consistent with observational data currently available. Future telescopes, however, should be capable of detecting the majority of these events, thereby confirming the existence of Population III binary remnants. Our model also implies the existence of massive star mergers with total masses between 40 and 100 solar masses in low-mass galaxy nuclei at redshift greater than 0. This could lead to a better understanding of heavy element formation in the early universe. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AstroTsuji/PaperCode. Our simulation data are also available at https://github.com/AstroTsuji/SimulationData.

To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the design of secure wireless communication systems using dual hop OFDM technology. System performance is evaluated using various metrics, and the findings are supported by numerical data presented in multiple figures and tables. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. Our experiments demonstrate that by increasing simulation speed, we can conduct statistically reliable tests with just a single agent, eliminating the need to run repeated trials. Our findings highlight the critical importance of speed when testing virtual agents and showcase the practical advantages of our optimized text-based game framework, which is available for free use by the research community. Our text-based game challenges are applicable to various applications, including teaching AI agents how to navigate complex worlds and evaluating the fairness of agent evaluation platforms. Our code is readily accessible on GitHub at this link https://github.com/agentscode/textworldexpress. Deep learning models, specifically LSTM architectures, have demonstrated superior performance in sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their extensive size. To address this challenge, this paper explores compact LSTM models, focusing on two subfields: model pruning and generative compact models. Initially, we review the most notable methods for LSTM model pruning and the current research on generating compact models using transfer learning and dense connections. Furthermore, three novel LSTM models are presented, each utilizing a distinct technique to produce a highly compact model for efficient sequence analysis. These models, known as S-LSTMs, are created using sparse structures that mimic the inherent characteristics of neural networks, with the goal of achieving comparable performance while significantly reducing model complexity. S-LSTMs consist of three types: models with sparse structures derived from non-linear thresholding, models with randomly induced sparsity, and models with structured sparsity based on differential evolution. These models exhibit substantial reductions in model size, with corresponding increases in inference speed, making them highly suitable for numerous sequence analysis applications. Experimental evaluations across six distinct datasets reveal the superior performance and efficiency of S-LSTMs in tasks such as sentiment analysis, stock market prediction, and biomedical text classification. S-LSTMs demonstrate a notable decrease in model size, with a average reduction of 89% in parameters, accompanied by notable improvements in accuracy, exceeding the performance of conventional LSTM models by an average of 12.5%. The source code for this study has been made available online at this link https://github.com/zwang95/SLSTM. Keywords: Long short-term memory networks, Model pruning, Generative compact models, Transfer learning, Dense connections, Neural network structure learning, Sequence analysis tasks.

These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validate the model's technical characteristics, while a previous research finding indicating larger redispatch orders could lead to increased costs in the market is also confirmed. The model's full source code is available at [link to repository]. The code can be utilized for conducting replicate analyses, as well as used as a foundation for conducting new research among the ancillary services and electricity market research community. The model comprises approximately 1,300 lines of Python code, in addition to approximately 1,000 lines of Cython code, and features well-structured, modular code that complies with professional standards. The model's parameters, input data, and results are managed through PyPSA's data structures, ensuring seamless integration with the PyPSA toolset, thereby enabling effortless execution of subsequent analyses through PyPSA, such as optimal expansion pathways calculations. The model's documentation is thorough, with explicit code explanations, as well as instructional guides for installing the required dependencies, generating results, and plotting performance indicators. The model's developers encourage feedback from potential users, as well as suggestions for improving the model, to ensure it remains a valuable resource for the research community. The code and model are collectively referred to as ASCAM, an open-source framework for evaluating design options for ancillary services and electricity markets through agent-based modeling. The ASCAM framework comprises the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model, the MESA-based clearing algorithms, the PyPSA toolset, as well as the PyPSA-YAML input data management system. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. Specifically, for a generic monic polynomial of degree d > 1 and its n-fold iterate, defined as the composition of n instances of said polynomial, its Galois group over rational numbers was found to be isomorphic to the symmetric group S_n. This result can be generalized to any field of characteristic zero with a given set of algebraic and architectural properties, as long as the polynomial's degree is a fixed integer greater than 1. To expand upon this, we examine a family of polynomial systems with varying parameters and coefficients within a specified polynomial family, mapped under the Galois group's action, which translates to permuting these parameters under the symmetric group S_n. By applying explicit formulae for the minimal subfields of a given field that contain specific subsets of its elements, we can determine the structure of these subfields as extensions of the base field, defined as the field generated by the polynomial system's parameters. Consequently, we can establish a direct relationship between these subfields and the group's permutation action, thereby establishing the connection between the Galois group of the n-fold iterate and the symmetric group S_n. Additionally, this analysis allows us to investigate the cohomological nature of these extensions and related 2-cocycles, which, in turn, enables us to describe the permutation group's actions in terms of 2-cocycles and their isomorphic classes. By exploring these 2-cocycles' properties, we can extract information about the field's architecture, specifically its "ramification depths" at certain prime numbers. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. Despite their significance, the mechanisms driving the formation of these vortices, known as polar vortices, remain poorly understood compared to those on Mars and Earth. A numerical model simulating Saturn's atmospheric circulation was used to analyze the behavior of the polar atmosphere between altitudes of 75 to 150 km above the cloud tops. The results show that the temperature variations within the polar vortices during the Saturnian spring and summer are insufficient to explain their formation, leading to the conclusion that other factors, specifically the movement of winds in the upper atmosphere, must be responsible. The model reveals that winds in the upper atmosphere, fueled by the migration of the sun, create massive vortex pairs at both poles, and these vortices move towards the equator as the year progresses. The model also indicates that the conditions necessary for the formation of broad, warm vortices in the polar stratosphere occur when the tilt of Saturn's axis causes its poles to tilt towards the sun, and this phenomenon has been confirmed using data from the Cassini spacecraft. Furthermore, the model explains the temperature gradients within the vortices, and these predictions match actual measurements taken during the Cassini era. Additionally, the model predicts seasonal variations of the vortices in the south polar stratosphere during the autumn and winter months, and these predictions await confirmation from future spacecraft observing Saturn's atmosphere. The model highlights the significance of considering the global atmospheric circulation when studying the polar stratosphere on Saturn, and it emphasizes the potential for future missions to uncover seasonal variations on both north and south poles using a combination of atmospheric circulation patterns. The model's limitations also underscore the potential for improving atmospheric circulation models by incorporating more detailed information about the atmospheric circulation on Saturn, specifically at higher altitudes above the cloud tops. The model's ability to accurately simulate the behavior of the polar vortices during the Saturnian spring and summer, in the stratosphere above the cloud tops, marks a significant advancement in the understanding of this phenomenon and paves the way for further research on the seasonal variations within the polar atmosphere on Saturn. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. A similar algorithm may be applicable to other x-ray experiments involving scattered light off atomic or nuclear components, and it offers scope for developing novel spectroscopic techniques that rely on phase information. Our research identifies potential for developing a generative model that can accurately predict M\"ossbauer spectra from experimental data, exceeding the performance of established methods like the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm by several orders of magnitude. As x-ray quantum optics continues to evolve, our approach may find application in experiments with increasing complexity that involve multiple scattering off atomic or nuclear components. Our code is available online for the benefit of the scientific community. A future direction for development involves exploring a generative model that can effectively utilize time- and energy-resolved x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei off a synchrotron radiation source, leading to a more accurate prediction of M\"ossbauer spectra, a task that remains challenging to the present day. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric outcomes with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach provides significantly improved convergence rates compared to other hybrid multi-phase flow models, under similar problem conditions. This knowledge can be useful for extending our model to accommodate two-phase flow scenarios. Our code is available for public use within the Feroxy repository. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. Utilizing Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, we conducted a series of simulations designed to assess the performance of Bayes factor estimates under various conditions, including different sample sizes and model specifications. Our results provide valuable insights into the performance of Bayes factor estimates and highlight potential limitations of the methods used, with implications for the practice of cognitive science. We also examine potential solutions to these limitations, including the use of flat prior distributions and the estimation of Bayes factors based on posterior predictive distributions. By exploring these challenges in a controlled environment, our research seeks to contribute to the methodological advancements in cognitive science, with applications across various fields, including psychology, economics, and linguistics. We anticipate that our findings will be beneficial for researchers and provide a framework for evaluating the validity of Bayes factor estimates in future studies. Systematic use of utility functions in decision-making is another significant aspect we are investigating, with an emphasis on the Bayesian approach, although our methods are compatible with other statistical frameworks. We intend to expand our research to other challenging computational problems involving Bayesian methods, with a focus on developing efficient solutions, evaluating the performance of these solutions through simulation-based methods, and exploring alternative solutions for notable challenges. We plan to make our software, including the Markov chain Monte Carlo methods used, publicly available to facilitate widespread use within the scientific community. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to associate each sentence with a set of suitable indicators, effectively extending the semantic information encoded in the model's sentence representations. By leveraging these indicators, the performance of classification tasks can be enhanced, with a notable improvement in cases where the relationship between sentences is crucial, such as in contrastive classification tasks. To facilitate reproducibility, the code and necessary datasets have been made publicly available, demonstrating the applicability of this approach to a broad range of classification tasks involving complex sentences. Experimental results show that the approach is particularly effective when the relationship between sentences is defined as contrasting or identical, with performance improvements of 8% and 12% respectively on existing datasets. Furthermore, the approach can be integrated into a generative adversarial contrastive learning framework, leading to a significant improvement of 18% in the recall rate for contrasting sentences. In addition, an analysis of the predicted indicators reveals their capability to capture subtle semantic relationships, with an example provided in the appendix. To further advance the field, potential research directions are proposed, such as utilizing part-of-speech tags and dependency parsing to refine the predicted indicators, as well as exploring the suitability of the approach for other languages. The models have been made available on Model Hub at the following address: https://modelhub.azurewebsites.com/models/semantic-discourse-indicators. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We demonstrate the applicability of these findings to a wide range of matrix optimization problems, including those with nonlinear objectives and constraints. Systematic simulations are conducted to validate the accuracy of our theoretical predictions and showcase the impact of different parameter settings. As a result, we offer specific recommendations for the implementation of vanilla gradient descent. To facilitate widespread access, we have made our simulation code publicly available. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In addition, our results provided specific guidance on parameter settings that influence the speed and efficiency of player learning in accordance with the structure of the particular Cournot model used. Ultimately, our research demonstrated robust convergence to a Nash Equilibrium using co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of models, dispelling earlier skepticism about the capacity of genetic algorithms for achieving NE in Cournot models. In doing so, we challenged initial doubts with a more rigorous approach, providing valuable insights for economists, game theory experts, and computational biologists alike. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following our previous study that demonstrated how activation clipping enhances robustness in convolutional neural networks, this paper builds upon that work by exploring other reliable data preprocessing methods, examining their individual and combined effects with activation clipping. Our findings reveal that in addition to the effects observed in our prior research, mean normalization can provide additional accuracy benefits when combined with activation clipping, while max normalization offers no significant gain. Our evaluation covers both clean and noisy data and across multiple precision levels, providing a comprehensive framework for practitioners seeking to deploy reliable and accurate CNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuang333/robust-cnn.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. In constructing this unified vocabulary space, we cluster words based on three key features: (1) their frequency of use in online comments, (2) the coherence they exhibit in text conversations, and (own a subfield known as monosemy, where a single word can have multiple distinct meanings). Ultimately, this singular vocabulary space empowers several exciting possibilities, including enhancing machine translation, identifying neologisms, and uncovering subtle semantic shifts in words over time. Our model performed exceptionally well in a range of evaluations, surpassing the outcomes of comparably complex models that operate within the confines of individual languages. Our code is available online for the benefit of the research community.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this, the model was modified to incorporate a feature mimicking the tendency of affected individuals to stay in areas with previous disorders, which significantly improved its ability to accurately depict the riots' spatial spread in Santiago. This revised model demonstrates its utility in predicting future rioting activity and estimating the influence of various factors on disorder distribution. By integrating transportation infrastructure into models of this type, researchers can gain a more nuanced understanding of the complex social phenomena driving urban unrest. This study's limitations provide a foundation for exploring related research questions in the future. The code and data for this project are available online. The original model that failed to capture Santiago's disorder distribution has been made available as well, offering a point of comparison for future similar analyses. This project was funded by the National Science Foundation, and the author would like to thank Dr. Nils Gessner for his assistance with code maintenance. This research was conducted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for a PhD in sociology from Duke University. The primary findings presented here were initially explored in a blog post published on the author's website. The revised model that succeeded in capturing the disorders' distribution in Santiago was discovered coincidentally, which led to a re-examination of the original model's limitations. The data and code for this project are available on GitHub, along with the code for the original model that failed to capture the disorders' distribution in Santiago. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. This results in a more efficient algorithm for containment determination, with a time complexity of $O(n^6)$ for containment assessment and $O(n^5)$ for the inclusion problem, where $n$ represents the number of nodes in the parse structure of a given regular expression. Furthermore, this research includes an example application of this containment algorithm for solving reachability analysis problems in regular models of communicating systems, where regular expression-based definitions of data formats or protocol specifications can handle infinite sets of recognizable characters, providing a valuable extension of existing methodology. A mock implementation of this algorithm is compared to standard methodologies for containment and inclusion assessment, demonstrating improved efficiency and a wider range of applicability. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been highly valued. These algorithms utilize simultaneous video and inertial data for precise pose estimation, and are particularly effective for mobile robots with monocular vision, aerial vehicles, and autonomous undersea vehicles. Existing VIO methods generally employ optimization-based or deep learning techniques, and often lack theoretical guarantees due to the challenging non-linear and continuous nature of orientation estimation. This study presents a novel orientation-aware graph-based VIO algorithm, utilizing inertial measurements to maintain orientation estimates, and incorporates a variance-aware re-weighting strategy to enhance robustness. Experimental results utilizing a monocular camera and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) on a quadcopter demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, with orientation RMSE below 0.25 rad and position RMSE below 0.43 m. By leveraging the properties of graph optimization and inertial measurements, this study's VIO algorithm provides a compelling alternative to conventional techniques, with orientation estimation applications in particular benefiting from the proposed method. System evaluation was conducted using a monocular camera and an IMU on a quadcopter, with orientation RMSE below 0.25 rad and position RMSE below 0.43 m. The algorithm's orientation-aware design offers particular advantages in environments with minimal parallax, such as on-board vehicles in industrial settings. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Specially, we predict that showy Weyl arms can be tuned into existence near the Fermi level in our proposed model. Moreover, the generation of SHOWS state is robust against various perturbations, ensuring the longevity of its unique square-root topological properties. Experimental verification of the SHOWS state can be achieved using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and transport measurements in ultra-pure samples made from layered honeycomb materials such as TaAs, PbTaO$_2$, and Graeme. Our theoretical framework also opens up possibilities for realizing square-root topological properties in other systems, such as 3D topological metals and superconductors. Schematically, SHOWS can be viewed as a bridge connecting Weyl semimetal and Dirac semimetal states. By adjusting the interlayer coupling strength, we can smoothly transform the SHOWS state into a 3D solid-state equivalent of the square-root Dirac semimetal model proposed previously. Our research provides a theoretical basis for experimental searches of square-root topological properties and predicts the energy ranges and robustness of the SHOWS state. Moreover, our proposed model offers actionable advice for creating showy Weyl arms near the Fermi level in 3D solid-state systems. Our theoretical findings can be verified by comparing the calculated band structures with experimental ARPES data from ultra-pure samples made from layered honeycomb materials. Our research demonstrates that Weyl semimetal state can be induced in materials with honeycomb structures through appropriate tuning of the interlayer coupling strength. By analyzing the robustness of showy Weyl arms against various perturbations, we can identify stable materials candidates for the SHOWS state. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, utilizing a quasi-reversibility method to handle the incomplete data. Specifically, we aim to recover missing boundary conditions on a subdomain of the boundary, where measurements are available, for the electric field and its derivative, given incomplete information on another subdomain of the boundary. Our approach employs a nonlinear inverse problem to determine the missing boundary conditions, which results in formulating an optimization problem. Nevertheless, this problem does not have a unique solution due to the lack of measurement data on certain boundary conditions, which hinders its direct solution. Consequently, we transform the problem into a minimization problem for the electric potential, which can be solved numerically using a finite element method. Additionally, we propose an alternative strategy based on the quasi-reversibility method, which provides a stable and second-order approximation to the original problem. This approach yields a system of time-harmonic Maxwell equations with nonhomogeneous anisotropic conductivity, which can be solved using a finite element method. Our numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy in reconstructing boundary conditions and the electric field, especially in scenarios with complex geometries and incomplete data on the boundary. Moreover, this approach can be extended to the three-dimensional case. Edmunds et al. initially introduced the quasi-reversibility method for solving the inverse problem of recovering the anisotropic conductivity in the time-harmonic Maxwell equations, which this study extends to the recovery of boundary conditions. Additionally, we propose a hybrid strategy based on the quasi-reversibility method and the nonlinear inverse problem formulation, which provides a more accurate solution to the inverse problem. This hybrid approach employs the solution from the nonlinear inverse problem as an initial condition for the quasi-reversibility method, which significantly improves the solution by closer alignment with the data, as verified by numerical experiments. Notably, this hybrid strategy enables the recovery of missing boundary conditions for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on incomplete measurements on the boundary, which cannot be solved using the quasi-reversibility method alone due to nonuniqueness. Nonetheless, due to nonuniqueness, we introduce Tikhonov regularization to ensure the existence of a solution. To address scalability issues in model training for high-dimensional data, we present the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) technique, tailored for linear models. FedSA divides the training process into two stages: initially, it conducts a standard federated learning procedure to create a global model, and subsequently, it performs selective data aggregation on participant-provided model outputs to produce the final model. Unlike traditional federated learning methods, FedSA does not involve calculating the gradient of the linear model or performing model updates among participants. This innovative approach enables selective data retention, reduces communication costs, and accommodates larger model sizes. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of FedSA in reducing communication expenses while maintaining performance comparable to standard federated learning methods, as validated by linear classification and regression experiments. Moreover, FedSA exhibits enhanced robustness in situations with significant data skewness. Our research showcases the FedSA technique as a versatile framework suitable for various linear model training settings, encompassing non-sparse models. To facilitate broad adoption, we have open-sourced the FedSA code.

This analysis applies to any unitary operator $\calC$ that acts on the boundary of the region and uses the definition of the energy-momentum tensor in relation to the change in entropy. As a specific example, we find that the properties of the unitary operator $\calC$ imply a condition on the energy-momentum tensor in the interior of the region, effectively moving the QNEC from the boundary to the interior.
